after: ## The five forms, each as a chain
alt: Five rows, one per form of globalisation, each as a three-step chain: specialisation (tea grown in volume at lower cost), relative cost advantage (assembly moved abroad, home jobs lost), movement of labour (skilled staff recruited from abroad), larger markets (exports to ten countries, lower unit cost) and international competition (cheaper imports force cost cuts or a niche).
caption: Learn each form as a cause-and-effect chain ending in an effect on the business.

after: ## Benefits and drawbacks: four different viewpoints
alt: A two-by-two grid of benefits and drawbacks of globalisation for businesses and economies in developed and developing countries, for example larger markets but low-cost rivals for a developed-country business, and new jobs but emigrating skilled workers for a developing economy.
caption: Who gains and who loses depends on the viewpoint.

after: ## Benefits and drawbacks: four different viewpoints
alt: A bare claim, “Globalisation is good”, earns little. A developed chain states the viewpoint (a developing-country garment maker), the cause (lower labour costs), the effect (large export orders) and the wider effect (local jobs).
caption: Name the viewpoint, then link cause to effect.

alt: A grid of exchange-rate effects. When the home currency strengthens, exporters’ goods cost more for foreign buyers so sales tend to fall, while importers’ costs fall. When it weakens, export sales tend to rise and importers’ costs rise.
caption: A stronger currency hurts exporters and helps importers; a weaker one does the reverse.

alt: Velden Ceramics made $120,000 profit (10,000 vases × $12). After the home currency strengthens, keeping the $30 price with sales of 8,500 gives $102,000; cutting to $27 keeps 10,000 sales at $9 each, $90,000. If sales under option A fell to 7,000, profit would be $84,000 and option B would be better.
caption: A stronger currency cuts either sales or profit per unit; which hurts less depends on buyers.

alt: A severe, sudden exchange-rate swing brings four problems: uncertain costs and revenues, difficult pricing, harder planning and lost contracts. Businesses reduce the risk by pricing in their own currency, buying from home suppliers and selling in several countries.
caption: Sudden swings make costs, prices and plans uncertain; spreading currencies reduces the risk.
